cls: Depolarising (non-competitive) neuromuscular blocking agent - skeletal muscle relaxant
pharm: An ultra-short-acting depolarising neuromuscular blocker used to facilitate tracheal intubation and provide skeletal muscle relaxation
quick: Intubation: 0.6 mg/kg IV (range 0.3-1.1 mg/kg); maintenance by intermittent dose or infusion
Used in obstetric anaesthesia; plasma cholinesterase lower in pregnancy
Single peri-operative dose; brief, minimal concern
Caution - avoid if hyperkalaemia/renal failure with high K+
Not relevant to single anaesthetic use
Continuous ventilation/airway, ECG, neuromuscular function, temperature (MH), potassium
summary: Succinylcholine chloride (suxamethonium) is an ultra-short-acting depolarising neuromuscular blocking agent used to produce skeletal muscle relaxation, principally to facilitate rapid tracheal intubation and during electroconvulsive therapy or short procedures. It acts at the neuromuscular junction by persistently depolarising the motor end-plate, causing transient fasciculations followed by flaccid paralysis, with rapid onset (about 30-60 seconds) and short duration (about 4-6 minutes) owing to hydrolysis by plasma (pseudo)cholinesterase. It carries a BOXED WARNING that in children and adolescents its use is generally restricted to emergency intubation or where immediate airway securing is necessary, because rare undiagnosed skeletal-muscle myopathy (e.g. Duchenne dystrophy) can cause acute rhabdomyolysis with hyperkalaemia, ventricular arrhythmia and cardiac arrest. It is also a potent trigger of malignant hyperthermia. It must be given only by those skilled in airway management with facilities for ventilation and resuscitation. Prolonged paralysis occurs in patients with atypical or deficient plasma cholinesterase.
indications: Adjunct to general anaesthesia to facilitate tracheal intubation
To provide skeletal muscle relaxation during surgery or mechanical ventilation
To reduce the intensity of muscle contractions during electroconvulsive therapy or pharmacologically/electrically induced convulsions

dosage.d: 0.6 mg/kg IV (usual range 0.3 to 1.1 mg/kg); for rapid sequence intubation often 1-1.5 mg/kg
Intermittent IV 0.04-0.07 mg/kg as needed, OR continuous infusion 2.5-4.3 mg/min (0.5-10 mg/min range) of dilute solution
dosage.n: Risk of phase II block and prolonged apnoea with high cumulative dose/infusion

dosage.d: Infants/small children up to 2 mg/kg IV; older children/adolescents 1 mg/kg IV; IM up to 3-4 mg/kg (max 150 mg) if no IV access
dosage.n: Restricted to emergency airway control; pretreat to attenuate bradycardia

dosage.d: Up to 3-4 mg/kg, not exceeding a total of 150 mg

admin: Administer only by personnel skilled in airway management, with immediate facilities for intubation, mechanical ventilation, oxygen and full resuscitation
Ensure adequate anaesthesia/sedation - succinylcholine does not produce unconsciousness or analgesia
Consider a small defasciculating dose of a non-depolarising agent and pretreatment with atropine (especially in children and with repeat doses) to limit fasciculations and bradycardia
Have dantrolene and a malignant-hyperthermia protocol immediately available; monitor temperature, capnography and ECG
Avoid in patients at risk of severe hyperkalaemia (e.g. major burns, crush/denervation injury, prolonged immobilisation, upper motor neuron lesions, pre-existing hyperkalaemia)
Anticipate prolonged paralysis in patients with atypical or low plasma (pseudo)cholinesterase; provide ventilation until recovery
moa: Succinylcholine consists of two acetylcholine molecules joined together and acts as a depolarising neuromuscular blocker. It binds nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the motor end-plate and, unlike acetylcholine, is not rapidly hydrolysed there, so it produces sustained depolarisation. This causes initial disorganised muscle contractions (fasciculations) followed by flaccid paralysis as the end-plate remains depolarised and the muscle becomes refractory (phase I block). Because it is not metabolised by acetylcholinesterase at the junction, its action is terminated by diffusion away and hydrolysis by plasma (pseudo)cholinesterase, giving its characteristically rapid onset and ultra-short duration. With high or repeated doses the block can convert to a phase II (desensitising) block.

absolute: Personal or familial history of malignant hyperthermia
Skeletal muscle myopathies (e.g. Duchenne muscular dystrophy)
Acute phase of major burns, multiple trauma, extensive denervation of skeletal muscle, or upper motor neuron injury (severe hyperkalaemia risk)
relative: Known or suspected atypical/reduced plasma (pseudo)cholinesterase activity
Penetrating eye injury or glaucoma (transient rise in intra-ocular pressure)
Conditions with raised intracranial or intragastric pressure
Severe sepsis, prolonged immobilisation, or chronic abdominal infection (up-regulated receptors, hyperkalaemia risk)
monitor: Body temperature and end-tidal CO2 for malignant hyperthermia
Serum potassium where hyperkalaemia is a concern

preg: Succinylcholine is commonly used to facilitate intubation in obstetric anaesthesia. Plasma cholinesterase activity is reduced in pregnancy and the early postpartum period, which can modestly prolong its effect. It is poorly lipid-soluble and minimally crosses the placenta at usual doses; use it when neuromuscular blockade is needed, with appropriate monitoring.
lact: A single peri-operative dose of succinylcholine is rapidly hydrolysed and breastfeeding can generally resume once the mother has recovered from anaesthesia. The brief exposure poses minimal risk to a breastfed infant.
renal: Succinylcholine itself does not require renal dose adjustment, but it should be avoided in patients with renal failure who have, or are prone to, hyperkalaemia because the potassium rise it causes can precipitate dangerous arrhythmias.
hepatic: Plasma (pseudo)cholinesterase is produced by the liver; severe hepatic disease can reduce enzyme levels and prolong neuromuscular blockade. Use with caution and be prepared to ventilate until full recovery.

major: Volatile anaesthetics (halothane, sevoflurane, etc.) - increase the risk of malignant hyperthermia when combined with succinylcholine
Drugs lowering plasma cholinesterase (e.g. echothiophate, organophosphates, neostigmine/anticholinesterases, cyclophosphamide) - markedly prolong paralysis
Digoxin/digitalis - succinylcholine can precipitate arrhythmias in digitalised patients (potassium shifts)
moderate: Aminoglycoside, polymyxin and other antibiotics with neuromuscular effects - potentiate and prolong block
Magnesium salts, lithium, lidocaine, beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers - may enhance neuromuscular blockade
Non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers - complex interaction; small defasciculating dose reduces fasciculations but may slightly reduce potency
minor: Oral contraceptives and some other drugs can modestly lower plasma cholinesterase
interactions.alcohol: Not relevant to single peri-operative use
interactions.diagnostics: Causes transient hyperkalaemia and can raise serum potassium; assess plasma cholinesterase (dibucaine number) where atypical enzyme is suspected

common: Muscle fasciculations and postoperative muscle pain/myalgia
Increased intra-ocular, intracranial and intragastric pressure
serious: Life-threatening hyperkalaemia with cardiac arrhythmia/arrest (especially burns, trauma, neuromuscular disease, children with occult myopathy)
Prolonged apnoea/paralysis in plasma-cholinesterase deficiency or phase II block
Severe bradycardia or asystole (particularly children and with repeat doses)
Anaphylaxis (succinylcholine is a leading cause of perioperative anaphylaxis)
rare: Masseter muscle rigidity (may herald malignant hyperthermia)
emergency: Malignant hyperthermia (rising end-tidal CO2, hyperthermia, rigidity) - give dantrolene, stop trigger

monitoring: ECG for bradycardia and hyperkalaemia-related arrhythmias
Neuromuscular monitoring (train-of-four) and confirmation of recovery before extubation
Body temperature and end-tidal CO2 for malignant hyperthermia
Serum potassium in patients at risk of hyperkalaemia; plasma cholinesterase if prolonged block occurs
counsel: This is a short-acting muscle relaxant given during anaesthesia to help place a breathing tube; you will be unconscious and breathing will be supported
You may have muscle aches for a day or two afterward, which is common and harmless
Tell your anaesthetist if you or any blood relative has ever had a severe high-temperature reaction (malignant hyperthermia) or unusually prolonged paralysis after anaesthesia
Report any family history of muscle disease or problems waking up after previous anaesthetics
It is given only in a monitored setting by trained staff
pk: Very rapid - paralysis within about 30-60 seconds after IV injection
Maximal neuromuscular block within about 1 minute
Extremely short; rapidly hydrolysed by plasma (pseudo)cholinesterase (effect dissipates within minutes)
Clinical relaxation about 4-6 minutes; spontaneous recovery in ~10 minutes (prolonged if cholinesterase deficient)
Store refrigerated (2-8 C); multidose vials may be kept at room temperature for a limited period per label; protect from heat
pearls: BOXED WARNING: in children/adolescents reserve for emergency intubation or securing the airway - undiagnosed myopathy (e.g. Duchenne) can cause acute rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia and cardiac arrest
Potent trigger of malignant hyperthermia - have dantrolene and an MH protocol immediately available; masseter rigidity may be an early sign
Avoid in burns, major trauma, denervation/upper motor neuron injury and prolonged immobilisation due to severe hyperkalaemia risk
Provides paralysis but NO sedation or analgesia - ensure adequate anaesthesia
Ultra-short action via plasma (pseudo)cholinesterase; atypical/deficient enzyme causes prolonged apnoea (ventilate until recovery; check dibucaine number)
Pretreat with atropine and consider a defasciculating dose to limit bradycardia and fasciculation-related myalgia; a leading cause of perioperative anaphylaxis
missed: Succinylcholine is administered only by anaesthesia/critical-care professionals during procedures, so there is no concept of a patient missed dose; dosing is titrated to clinical effect under continuous monitoring.
overdose: Overdose causes prolonged neuromuscular paralysis and apnoea. Management is supportive: maintain a patent airway and continue controlled mechanical ventilation with oxygen until spontaneous respiration and neuromuscular function fully recover. Anticholinesterases do NOT reverse and may worsen a phase I depolarising block; treat associated bradycardia with atropine and manage hyperkalaemia and any malignant hyperthermia (dantrolene) promptly.
